newsitem.title: USA: S.C. lawmakers worry about road funding.
newsitem.headline: S.C. lawmakers worry about road funding.

text.p: South Carolina lawmakers are hinting that the state gasoline tax may need to be increased to raise an extra $14 billion in funds to pay for road and bridge repairs over the next two decades, The State newspaper reported on Monday.

"I think that for the first time in several years, there's a realizatin that we have to figure out something," House Speaker David Wilkins said. "I think there's a willingness to listen to all possibilities."
Last week, the Greenville Chamber of Commerce endorsed a proposal to charge tolls to pay for widening Interstate highway 85.

A growing number of state politicians are privately talking about whether the state's 16 cent per gallon gasoline tax needs to be raised, the newspaper reported. A penny increase in the gasoline tax would raise an estimated $21 million to $25 million.
Governor David Beasley has said he opposes any tax hike.

South Carolina needs about $24 billion during the next 20 years for road and bridge projects. That's about $14 billion more than the state is expected to receive in taxes and other projected revenues, officials said.

Some lawmakers have proposed a $1.2 billion bond plan to pay for the road repairs. But the plan faces opposition because it calls for linking part of growth in state revenues to pay for the bonds, which could squeeze other state programs and exhaust most of the state's credit line, according to state senator Arthur Ravenel.
Gov. Beasley was scheduled to issue his proposed 1997-98 budget next week, which should address the road funding issues.
